newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe to bar foreigners from owning land.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe to bar foreigners from owning land.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe said on Tuesday he would soon expand a controversial land acquisition law to include an agricultural tax and bar foreigners and companies from owning land.

In an address to a new session of the parliament of Zimbabwe, Mugabe also said his 17-year-old government would, in the coming year, sub-divide large-scale farms into small commercial holdings to enable easy entry of the country's black majority into commercial agriculture.

Mugabe's government has acquired about three million hectares of land, mostly from white commercial farmers, since 1992 under a controversial Land Acquisition Act that allows it to forcibly buy farms to resettle landless black peasants.

Zimbabwean whites, who ruled the southern African state before independence in 1980, occupy most of the fertile land but some of the land they were forced to surrender for the peasant resettlement scheme is now being leased by leading state officials, including cabinet ministers.
On Tuesday Mugabe said his government still intended to buy over five million more hectares to fulfill its resettlement plans.

"In the area of agrarian reform, the government will implement the recommendations of the Land Tenure Commission by introducing a new Land Act which will encompass a number of existing acts pertaining to land," he told the 150-member parliament in which his ruling ZANU-PF party occupies 147 seats.

"The new act will provide for the agricultural land tax and regulations that pertain to minimum farm sizes, adoption of one-man one-farm concept and the prohibition of ownership of land by foreigners and companies," he added, giving no further details.
Agriculture is one of the key pillars of Zimbabwe's economy, contributing an annual average of about 20 percent to its gross domestic product (GDP).

Mugabe has over the years bulldozed controversial policies in the farming sector, dismissing arguments that they were slowly damaging the economy on grounds that the measures were meant to benefit the country's majority poor blacks.
Some of the measures have included a 10 percent levy on tobacco, of which Zimbabwe is the second largest exporter after Brazil.

Mugabe said on Tuesday earnings from agricultural exports would rise by 27 percent to Z$13.5 billion (U.S.$1.2 billion) this year following a good rainy season (November-April), and help consolidate its reform plans. $1 = Z$11.39
